title: Introduction to Information Security
subject: Information Security
summary: This module introduces information security, covering its history from early mainframes through the development of ARPANET and the Internet, key concepts like the CIA triad, critical characteristics of information, and organizational roles in implementing security.

nodes.label: Information Security
nodes.desc: The protection of information and its critical elements, including systems and hardware that use, store, and transmit that information.

nodes.label: History of Information Security
nodes.desc: Evolution from early mainframe physical security through ARPANET development, addressing vulnerabilities in password structures and remote access controls.

nodes.label: ARPANET
nodes.desc: The precursor to the Internet, developed by ARPA, which grew in popularity and revealed fundamental security problems requiring improved controls.

nodes.label: CIA Triad
nodes.desc: The standard security model consisting of Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability as the three key security objectives.

nodes.label: Critical Characteristics of Information
nodes.desc: Key attributes including confidentiality, integrity, availability, accuracy, authenticity, utility, and possession that determine information's value.

nodes.label: Key Security Concepts
nodes.desc: Fundamental terms including access, asset, attack, control, exploit, exposure, loss, risk, threat, vulnerability, and subjects/objects.

nodes.label: CISO
nodes.desc: Chief Information Security Officer with primary responsibility for assessment, management, and implementation of information security in the organization.

nodes.label: Information Security Project Team
nodes.desc: A functional team including champion, team leader, policy developers, risk specialists, security professionals, administrators, and end users.

nodes.label: Data Responsibilities
nodes.desc: Roles including data owners (senior management), data custodians (infrastructure guardians), data trustees (appointed overseers), and data users (access holders).

nodes.label: Top-Down Approach
nodes.desc: Security implementation initiated by upper management with policies, procedures, and formal development strategies like SDLC.

nodes.label: Bottom-Up Approach
nodes.desc: Grassroots security efforts by systems administrators working to improve system security without formal organizational support.

nodes.label: MULTICS
nodes.desc: Early operating system developed with security integrated into core functions, influencing the creation of UNIX and modern security concepts.

nodes.label: CNSS Security Model
nodes.desc: Committee on National Security Systems three-dimensional model with confidentiality, integrity, and availability as key security objectives.

nodes.label: Balancing Security and Access
nodes.desc: Security as a balance between protection and availability, recognizing that perfect security is impossible and access must be reasonable.

nodes.label: Communities of Interest
nodes.desc: Groups within organizations united by similar interests including information security management, IT professionals, and organizational management.

nodes.label: Key Dates in Information Security
nodes.desc: Important historical documents and developments from 1968-1992 including RAND Report R-609, TCSEC, and IPSEC protocols.

nodes.label: Information System Components
nodes.desc: The complete set of hardware, software, data, people, procedures, and networks that enable business information use.

nodes.label: Security as Art vs Science
nodes.desc: Debate over whether security implementation is an art (no universal solutions) or science (technology-based with specific conditions).
